So, Cauê, you’ve been to the States before, right?
Yes, to Orlando, at the beginning of the year. But to be honest, I wish I had used more English there.
Really? Didn’t you have to speak English all the time?
Not really. It was a Brazilian bubble. In every store, someone was speaking Portuguese, so we all stuck together.
That happens here in Toronto too. When I arrived, I only spoke to people from my city for months. I felt out of place everywhere else.
In hindsight, it was a missed opportunity. I wish I had talked to more locals.
Well, if only everybody looked back on a trip and learned something! What would you do differently next time?
I’d leave the bubble on day one, and make the most of every conversation. And I wish I could tell jokes in English. That’s my next goal.

Every city in the world has a bubble. Go to Lisbon, Bangkok or Orlando, and you'll find groups of people from the same country who stick together. I understand why. It's comfortable. Same language, same jokes, same food. When you feel out of place, the bubble feels like home. I did it myself. My first year in Madrid, I spent every weekend with other British people. In hindsight, it was a huge missed opportunity. I wish I'd learned Spanish faster. I wish I'd said yes to more invitations from locals. So here's my advice. In your first week, make one local friend. Just one. It changes everything.

When I moved to Brazil for work, I didn't speak a word of Portuguese. For the first few months, I only spoke English, with other foreigners. We went to the same restaurants and the same bars. It was easy, and it was a bubble. Looking back, I wish I'd taken Portuguese classes from the first week. If only someone had told me how much I was missing! Brazilians are so friendly, and I just couldn't talk to them properly. And one funny thing: I wish people would answer me in Portuguese. Every time I tried, they switched to English to be nice. Now I make the most of every chance to practice.

Most tourists never really see the city. They go from one tourist trap to the next, and they only talk to the hotel staff. So, my advice. First, ask a local where they eat, and go there. The food is better and cheaper. Second, don't worry about blending in. You'll stand out anyway, with your accent and your camera, and that's fine. People like it when you try. And third, if you feel homesick after a week or two, that's completely normal. The best cure isn't calling home. It's talking to people. When you look back on the trip, those conversations are what you'll remember.
